sentences.text: According to the program, the M4 on display was pulled from a Normandy field in 1998 and restored by volunteers over eleven years. Steel treads chewed the fresh asphalt on Elm, leaving herringbone scars the city council would grumble about for weeks. Smoke from the grain elevator drifted across the studio shot all afternoon. Analysts identified the vehicles as tracked self-propelled howitzers, most likely 2S19s, moving north in groups of three. Under the stoplight an M3 half-track idled, its white star freshly stenciled over decades of repainted olive drab. Ninety-one and ramrod straight, the parade marshal refused the golf cart and walked every block of the route. Checkpoint after checkpoint, each one slower and more suspicious than the last. "Back to you in the studio — we're hearing outgoing artillery again," Marisol shouted over the rotor noise. Did you see the turret swing toward the courthouse when the crew waved at the mayor? Civilians lined the shoulder in silence; one old man raised two fingers at the passing armor, and nobody could say what he meant. Members of VFW Post 214 led the procession down Main Street, trailed by a color guard and two armored personnel carriers on loan from the museum. By dawn the correspondents had relocated to a rooftop overlooking the bridge, where engineers were laying pontoon sections under sporadic fire. At the edge of town, a boy on a bicycle races the lead vehicle for a hundred meters, then peels away laughing. "They came through at three in the morning," the baker said, still in his apron, flour on his hands. The uplink kept dropping every time the jamming trucks rolled by, so we filed the package over a landline from the hotel basement. Rain threatened all morning, but by the time the armored column reached Third Street the sun broke through above the courthouse elms. Behind the drum line, a lone bagpiper played while names were read aloud at the memorial fountain. I counted the seconds between the flash on the ridge and the thud that rattled our satellite truck: eleven. You hear the squeal of steel tracks on asphalt long before the first hull crests the overpass. "Cover your ears, honey," a father said, hoisting his daughter as the howitzer crew readied the ceremonial salute. Dust from the tracks hangs over Highway 4 like a curtain nobody asked for. Officials declined to confirm how many armored personnel carriers crossed the river, citing operational security, though our footage shows at least nineteen. How long can the checkpoint hold, our anchor asked, and the reporter on the ground simply shrugged into the lens. Tracer fire stitched the dark behind the correspondent, who never once broke off her sentence. Between the honor guard and the antique jeeps came a flatbed carrying three men who had waded ashore at Omaha Beach. You could feel the tracks through the sidewalk before the vehicle ever rounded the corner by the pharmacy. The armored column stretched past the burned-out gas station, and our camera crew counted forty vehicles before soldiers waved us back. We staked out our spot by the drugstore at seven, thermoses full, lawn chairs sagging, two hours before the first unit stepped off. A Korean War nurse rode in the lead convertible, waving a gloved hand at people who were not yet born when she shipped out. Its Continental radial engine backfired twice near the reviewing stand, startling a pair of police horses. Flags in every fist, from the hardware store clear down to the savings and loan. Kids scrambled for candy tossed from the turret hatch, ignoring their mothers' shouted warnings about the moving treads. Somebody's selling commemorative pins near the reviewing stand, and the line already stretches past the hardware store awning. A vendor hawks miniature flags at two dollars apiece while the high school band tunes up behind the fire station. A correspondent in a flak jacket knelt beside the guardrail, whispering her stand-up while the convoy idled behind her. Popcorn, diesel, brass polish — the smell of the whole morning, honestly. The crowd went quiet as the riderless horse passed; even the vendors stopped calling out. Next year they'll widen the route, the mayor promises, so the half-tracks won't have to squeeze past parked cruisers on Oak. Tonight's broadcast opened with thermal footage of the convoy fording the shallows below the destroyed bridge. Honestly, the weirdest part is the ice cream vendor still working the intersection while turrets swivel past him. What is the meaning of the word tank?
